SMOKERS’ CORNER: THE AGE OF POLITICAL ABSURDITY. More than ever, modern political leaders across the globe are issuing statements that defy logic, science and history. Yet, instead of facing ridicule, these figures are frequently met with applause from their supporters. Last week, when Polish foreign minister Radosaw Sikorski claimed that Poland could swiftly defeat Russia in a direct conflict, political commentators across the United States and Europe met his remarks with mild mockery. However, within Poland, social media exploded with enthusiastic endorsement. Rather than facing critical pushback, Sikorski’s exaggerated claim was embraced as gospel by supporters. This perfectly illustrates how readily absurd political rhetoric is now absorbed. In a 2019 interview, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, while discussing India’s air strikes against Pakistan, explained that he advised military officials to launch the attack despite heavy rain and cloud cover. He ‘reasoned’ that clouds would block Pakistani radars. Even though radars operate via radio waves rather than visual sight, his supporters championed the assertion as an example of “military genius.” Modi’s historical claims are often even more surreal, such as his declaration that the birth of Karna in the ancient epic Mahabharata proves that test-tube baby technology was invented in ancient India. In a live 2021 television QnA, former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan attributed rising sexual violence to women wearing “vulgar” clothes. He argued that “men are not robots” and that “if a woman wears very few clothes, it will have an impact on the men.” When he was criticised by women activists, his supporters (including many women) rallied around him, asserting that his critics were trying to undermine “traditional cultural values.” In an age of algorithmic outrage, identity politics and collapsing trust in institutions, the most outrageous claims can become expressions of loyalty and powerful instruments of persuasion Following the Taliban’s takeover of Kabul in 2021, Khan praised the event, declaring that the Afghan people had “broken the shackles of slavery.” The statement ignored the ensuing human rights crises while framing a complex geopolitical takeover as a glorious anti-imperialist victory. Many of his supporters applauded his ‘bold’ statement. During the global Covid vaccination drive in 2021, then-Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro warned citizens that taking the Pfizer vaccine could cause people to turn into alligators and make women grow beards. His core evangelical support base accepted this without hesitation. In the US, Donald Trump remains a master of uttering similar hogwash. During his first presidency, he dismissed global warming threats by claiming that rising sea levels would simply create “more oceanfront properties.” He reduced a complex ecological crisis to a real estate opportunity while ignoring basic coastal geography. His supporters praised his insightfulness. Illustration by Abro These are just a handful of examples highlighting a shift in modern political discourse. This move from facing ridicule for spouting outright nonsense to this nonsense enjoying widespread applause is the result of some drastic changes in media ecosystems, societal psychology and the nature of modern political power. The primary engine driving the acceptance of absurd statements is what the American academic Dan Kahan calls “identity-protective cognition.” According to Kahan, when political identity becomes tightly tied to a group, individuals process information not to evaluate its objective truth but to protect their status within the group. Accepting an absurd claim made by the group’s leader confirms an individual’s loyalty to the group, whereas rejecting the claim means aligning with political opponents. Research led by the American professor of psychology and neural science Jay Van Bavel suggests that political loyalty in this regard acts as a “cognitive filter.” It overrides basic critical thinking and yields psychological rewards that reinforce one’s sense of belonging to a group, even when a leader’s claim contradicts reality. Historically, mainstream media often acted as gatekeepers. A ridiculous statement was processed through editorial standards, highlighted for its absurdity and derided on public platforms. Western media used to take apart various leaders for this — for instance, leaders such as Uganda’s dictator Idi Amin, who was reduced to being a joker, and Libya’s Muammar Gaddafi. Now the same West is struggling to comprehend mouthy far-right leaders in its own backyard. In Pakistan, Pir Pagara was often treated as a jester for making outlandish political predictions. Cartoonists often showed him with a parrot. Altaf Hussain was another politician who was regularly satirised and ridiculed, even though, to his followers he was a ‘visionary’. Till the 1990s, such characters were exceptions. Today, they are a norm. The rise of algorithmic platforms has gradually dismantled the role of gatekeepers. Various studies show that repeated exposure to a statement increases its perceived truthfulness, regardless of how implausible it sounds. Social media algorithms prioritise outrageous content because it drives engagement, causing absurd claims to be repeated millions of times in digital echo chambers. Studies by psychologists Gordon Pennycook and David Rand on misinformation show that repetition lowers a reader’s analytical guard, transitioning statements from sounding ridiculous to familiar and, eventually, to plausible and true. There are also studies that suggest that politicians, especially contemporary populists, do not utter absurdities by accident. They use them strategically. In their Rand Corporation paper on propaganda techniques, researchers Christopher Paul and Miriam Matthews coined the term “firehose of falsehood” to describe this “strategic disorientation.” The goal of flooding public space with continuous and blatantly absurd claims is not necessarily to convince everyone that a lie is true. It is used to exhaust the public’s capacity for critical thought. When politicians regularly spout absurdities, fact-checkers become overwhelmed. Academics at the global research network Evidence in Governance and Politics found that politicians, such as Trump, who aggressively dismiss corrections as ‘fake news’ retain public support and attention by sowing doubt about the mainstream media and fact-checkers themselves. Mouthy populist leaders are still roundly satirised, though. But when they routinely cross into surreal territory, satire loses its power. German-American political theorist Hannah Arendt wrote in The Origins of Totalitarianism that the ideal subjects of totalitarian rule are people for whom the distinction between fact and fiction no longer exists. When public trust in actual experts and state institutions collapses, expert consensus is no longer seen as a benchmark for truth. Instead, expertise is reframed as an establishment conspiracy. In this environment, an absurd statement from an ‘anti-establishment’ politician is perceived not as ignorance but as ‘bold defiance’ against a ‘corrupt’ system. The shift from ridiculing absurd political statements to believing them marks a transition from fact-based politics to identity-based politics. When an absurd claim is made, it serves as a flag planted by a leader in the ground. Followers do not process it through a filter asking if it is logically true. Instead, they spend more energy in contemplating which side they belong to if they accept or reject the claim. Until the dynamics and incentives of social media algorithms change and trust in shared institutions is restored, political absurdity will continue to erode as a punchline. Instead, it will solidify as a rather dangerous instrument of persuasion. Published in Dawn, EOS, September 27th, 2026

ATC acquits 7 more policemen ‘for lack of evidence’ in Naqeebullah Mehsud's murder case. KARACHI: After the acquittal of former Malir SSP Rao Anwar, an antiterrorism court on Saturday acquitted seven more policemen in a case over the killing of Naqeebullah Mehsud and three others in a staged encounter in January 2018. The then SHOs of Shah Latif Town and Sachal police, Amanullah Marwat and Shaikh Muhammad Shoaib alias Shooter; assistant sub-inspector (ASI) Gada Hussain; head constables Sadaqat Ali and Mohsin Abbasi; and constables Raja Shamim and Rana Riaz Ahmed were facing trial for allegedly killing Naseemullah, better known as Naqeebullah Mehsud, Mohammad Sabir, Nazar Jan and Mohammad Ishaq in an alleged staged encounter in January 2018. After examining the witnesses and hearing concluding arguments from both sides, the judge of ATC-VI exonerated the accused persons for lack of evidence. Prosecutor Anila Malik argued that the prosecution examined over 40 witnesses, including star witnesses and they linked the accused persons with the commission of offences and documentary evidence also corroborated their testimonies. Former SSP Rao Anwar was acquitted in the same case in 2023 She also contended that the prosecution established its case against all the accused persons beyond a shadow of reasonable doubt and pleaded for conviction. However, defence lawyer Farzana Mateen submitted that all accused persons facing trial were framed with mala fide intention and that out of 40, not a single witness directly implicated any of the accused in the case. She also maintained that there were glaring contradictions in the evidence of prosecution witnesses while two star witnesses about the abduction of Hazrat Ali and Muhammad Qasim did not associate the present accused persons in their statements recorded under Section 164 CrPC by a judicial magistrate and had also not identified these accused persons as the culprits during their evidence before the trial court. The defence lawyer further argued that there was no allegation of abduction of the deceased against the accused persons and the prosecution has also failed to prove their participation in the alleged encounter. She maintained that many accused persons, including a former senior superintendent of police, had already been exonerated by the trial court in the first round of litigation for want of evidence and she pleaded for acquittal of the present accused persons as well. Initially, the then SSP Malir Rao Anwar, along with his around two dozen subordinates, had been booked for allegedly murdering Naqeebullah and others in an alleged staged encounter in a Malir locality and dubbing them as militants. According to the prosecution, Naqeebullah was picked up with his two friends allegedly by eight to nine subordinates of Rao Anwar in civvies. Later, the other two detainees were set free while the whereabouts of Mehsud remained unknown and his mobile phone was also found powered off, as the former SSP allegedly kept him in wrongful detention. It further stated that on Jan 17, the captive’s relatives came to know through the media that Rao Anwar and his associates allegedly killed Mehsud and three others in a staged encounter in a Shah Latif Town area on Jan 13 and dubbed them as Taliban militants. The provincial police officer had constituted a three-member inquiry committee that found Rao Anwar and his associates involved in the case, it added. However, in January 2023, the trial court acquitted the former SSP and 17 members of his team by extending the benefit of doubt. As the state had opted not to impugn the acquittal order, a brother of Naqeeb had filed an appeal before the Sindh High Court against their acquittal. The present accused persons were absconders during the first trial, and after the exoneration of SSP and others, they had surrendered before the court to face the trial, and all of them were set free on bail in April this year. Progress at UNGA. ALTHOUGH no breakthrough was achieved at the UN General Assembly, there has been some progress where finding a negotiated solution to the US war on Iran is concerned. For example, both the American and Iranian delegations held talks mediated by Qatar, while the Iranian president told Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif that Tehran was still committed to the Islamabad MoU. Moreover, other reports indicate that both the US and Iran are looking for an off-ramp, with Tehran offering to open the Strait of Hormuz for marine traffic if Washington ends its blockade of Iran. The key question is: who will blink first in this battle of wits, as neither side will want to appear weak? Now it is up to both sides — as well as the states mediating this conflict — to take forward the progress made in New York. As the US, along with Israel, initiated this aggression, it should take the first step and offer confidence-building measures to Iran in order to de-escalate the situation and come to a long-term settlement. Though White House officials have said Iran is ‘desperate’ for a deal, the fact is that high fuel prices are also hurting the Trump administration at home. An unpopular war coupled with high inflation is not likely to have a positive effect on the Republicans’ chances going into November’s midterm elections. In a meeting on the UNGA sidelines, Mr Trump’s Gulf allies reportedly asked him for a post-midterm strategy regarding Iran. Perhaps something can come out of the interactions at the UN. However, the talks must not be a ruse to open Hormuz and to merely suspend hostilities and stabilise oil prices until the US midterms. There are some indications that the Trump administration may be considering kinetic action after the elections. It would mean a disastrous new confrontation in the Middle East. Hopefully, wiser counsel will prevail in Washington. The way forward seems simple. The US must approach Iran with sincerity, and the talks must not be a smokescreen for further military action later. The blockade of Iran should be lifted and its funds released to enable a longer-term peace. Tehran, on its part, should commit to keeping Hormuz open in the interest of both its neighbours and the wider international community, while also refraining from targeting the Gulf states. Also, any new agreement should cover all fronts: Gaza, Lebanon and Yemen. Although these are separate conflicts, they are also interlinked as Iranian allies are involved in all of them fighting Israel, the US and Saudi Arabia. Hence, a peace treaty with Iran alone may not last unless there is also calm in other regional theatres, while there is a particular need to rein in Israel’s murderous attacks on regional states. Four dialysis patients test positive for HIV at Mian Channu hospital. LAHORE: Four patients undergoing dialysis at the Tehsil Headquarters Hospital (THQ), Mian Channu, have tested positive for HIV, raising fresh concerns about infection-control practices at healthcare facilities in south Punjab. According to the reports available with Dawn , the patients, including three women, who had been receiving dialysis at the hospital tested positive for the deadly virus after initial diagnosis. The hospital administration has referred them to the Nishtar Hospital Multan for further medical evaluation and treatment and they are currently under treatment there. The Mian Channu hospital officials told the media that more than 60 patients were receiving dialysis at the facility and HIV could not be transmitted through the dialysis process. They said that they were assessing the situation. Infected patients, including three women, sent to Multan’s Nishtar Hospital Sources, however, said that more dialysis patients might also have tested positive but the officials did not confirm more cases. In recent years, several HIV cases were reported in the healthcare facilities in Punjab. In November 2024, around 30 kidney patients at the Nishtar Hospital were reported to have contracted HIV during dialysis, while one patient died after developing complications. A Punjab government fact-finding committee subsequently confirmed an HIV/AIDS outbreak in the hospital’s nephrology unit and identified violations of dialysis guidelines and standard operating procedures. A scientific study published in 2026, involving researchers from the Aga Khan University and the Punjab AIDS Control Programme, found that the Multan dialysis cases were closely linked and provided evidence that the infections originated within the healthcare setting. The Punjab government ordered proceedings under the PEEDA Act against senior officials and medical staff over alleged negligence and mismanagement related to the outbreak in Nishtar Hospital Multan in January 2025. Another major HIV-related crisis had emerged in Taunsa where 106 children tested HIV positive and they were registered with the AIDS Control Programme in March 2025. The government had established a screening and treatment centre at the THQ hospital and ordered action against senior local health officials. Later, a joint mission involving WHO, Unicef, UNAIDS and other partners carried out door-to-door screening of around 50,000 people in the affected area. It also said auto-disable syringes were supplied to government hospitals and that hundreds of clinics allegedly being run by quacks were sealed. The Punjab AIDS Control Programme says it provides free HIV testing, counselling, treatment, diagnostic services and follow-up care and treatment centres were established in districts, including Lahore, Multan and Dera Ghazi Khan, and more than 14,000 patients were receiving free treatment. At the federal level, the National AIDS Control Programme says 84,421 HIV cases were registered in Pakistan by December 2025, of whom 60,785 were receiving antiretroviral therapy at 98 centres. A broken power accord. ALTHOUGH the PTI has postponed its protest march on Islamabad, the capital city’s container-blocked roads continue to reflect the country’s deeper crisis. The crisis is not merely political, economic, or security-related; it is rooted in an elite class that cannot forge an accord within themselves. Islamabad is not witnessing a siege-like situation for the first time; it has become part of life for the inhabitants of the twin cities. Even a cricket match or a visiting dignitary can bring life to a standstill. Despite huge investments in infrastructure and expensive surveillance systems, the security providers remain nervous. They have turned the federal capital into a city of checkpoints, where the average citizen must pass through long queues every 10 minutes during his daily commute — with police officers regarding him with suspicious eyes. Citizens end up feeling that they themselves are responsible for all the country’s ills, while those who have actually encroached on green belts, footpaths, and even highways escape punishment for crimes they do not even understand. The crisis runs deep, and even the postponement of the protest by the PTI, and earlier by the Jamaat-i-Islami , will not solve the country’s political, governance, economic, and security crisis. These lines may seem cynical, but the streets of the federal capital tell Pakistan’s whole story. The ‘container-ment’ approach shows serious fractures among the power elites over the division of power, which has not been shared proportionately and has, in fact, caused a chronic political crisis and led to a rent-seeking economy. Rent-seeking means economic actors become adept at obtaining privileged access to the state or controlling scarce resources. The masses are not responsible for the country’s state of affairs; it is fractured power elites who have yet to learn the art of distributing power among themselves. Here, another term needs explaining. The ‘fractured elite’ comprises Pakistan’s dominant political, civil-military, judicial, and institutional elite — sometimes referred to as the establishment — when it no longer agrees on the basic rules of the political game. The elite includes religious and ideological authorities, but in an evolving power order, their role and share have been minimised for now. Major businesses and landed interests have become important actors within the fractured power order. Serious fractures exist among the elites over the division of power. A question arises: what does an elite power accord look like? Is it about who will have the political power to govern, and under what conditions? Another question emerges: aside from political power, who holds the real power, also referred to as institutional power? Does this authority belong to parliament, the executive, the military, the judiciary, or the bureaucracy? Institutional power brings control over major economic resources and rents, as well as coercive or security institutions. It also has territorial power to determine how the interests of the centre and the provinces are accommodated. Among the elites, succession remains a key question: how will power change hands? A linked challenge arises. How are influential groups accommodated? Foreign policy remains the exclusive domain of the power elites — what strategic interests are considered non-negotiable? Now look at the Pakistani elites, which have failed to define the role of political power. Gradually, an institution has assumed authority, while the ruling political parties have surrendered several rights to retain power. The opposition, meanwhile, is demanding its legitimate rights. Many political analysts arguably contend that the opposition, now led by the PTI, along with smaller parties within the opposition alliance, the Tehreek-i-Tahaffuz-i-Ayeen-i-Pakistan, is struggling for power rather than restoring or developing a new social contract in the country. Maulana Fazlur Rahman’s JUI-F is also part of the opposition. It has been marginalised in the power structure because the changing rules in the power playbook leave less space for religious actors now. The political power structure has clearly failed to advance nationhood, and power remains confined to one major influential ethnic group in the country. Those who represent the power structure in the public discourse and the social and mainstream media malign less powerful and marginalised groups, suggesting they go to Afghanistan — their remarks target both the Pakhtuns and the Baloch. They stigmatise the Kashmiris as well, who have been demanding their rights in Azad Kashmir. If state propagandists are suggesting a course of action for them, where are they supposed to go? Fractured power elites cannot create cohesion within a nation. They cannot resolve their internal discord, so how can they devise a broad formula for national cohesion? In their paranoid view, security has taken over dialogue, and they have grown accustomed to killing an ant with a hammer. Even when clear indications show dialogue is the best policy, power elites know it would mean accommodating new members in the power club and remain hesitant to admit newcomers. A lack of flexibility or capacity for dialogue creates a need for a hyper-coercive internal security order. An internal security review is underway to make it more coercive. KP has resisted somewhat by introducing the Police Act, 2026, which will bring provincial government oversight over the system, as was required in the KP context, where discord between the police and other institutions has become challenging. But the federal government is resisting it. It seems the power elites will not compromise on the new internal security order and will continue to push their agenda through Nacta or the interior ministry. Foreign policy and geopolitics are sensitive domains for public discourse in the country. The parameters of non-negotiable interests continue to blur and narrow. For the masses, the crisis in the country is no more than a long, tragic soap opera on screen, which they can watch, cry over, and laugh at, but cannot act on. The writer is a security analyst. The Houthi blockade. IN July 2026, the Houthis declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia, targeting Saudi-linked shipping, and warning commercial vessels of any nationality against calling at Saudi ports. Vessels deemed to breach the blockade faced attack wherever they entered the Houthis’ operational reach. Attacks on Saudi tankers and energy infrastructure were followed by traffic through Bab al-Mandeb falling to its lowest level in months. By September, Houthi forces had seized strategic islands around Bab al-Mandeb and gained control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, increasing their capacity to threaten, disrupt and potentially control maritime traffic through the strait. The conventional legal position is that naval blockade is a belligerent right associated with international armed conflict (IAC), mainly because it permits interference with neutral commercial shipping. As per this view, a non-state armed group engaged solely in a non-international armed conflict does not ordinarily have the authority to impose a blockade that is binding on neutral vessels. However, customary international law does not conclusively foreclose blockade in a sufficiently intense NIAC, particularly where an organised armed group exercises extensive territorial and governmental control and can enforce maritime restrictions. This question is particularly significant in Yemen, where there is a strong argument that the Houthis function as a de facto governmental authority rather than merely an insurgent movement. They have long controlled Sana’a, govern territory containing a substantial population, and have expanded along the Red Sea coast and around Bab al-Mandeb. Crucially, under the ICRC approach, effective governmental control, rather than global recognition alone, is central to determining de facto governmental authority. If the Houthis are treated as exercising Yemen’s governmental authority, their external hostilities may be characterised as those of Yemen itself, strengthening the argument that the relevant conflicts are international and that traditional belligerent rights, including blockade, are potentially available. Even if this characterisation is rejected, other factors point towards possible internationalisation. Saudi Arabia is directly engaged alongside the internationally recognised Yemeni authorities against the Houthis, while the latter have repeatedly attacked Saudi territory. Saudi intervention by invitation does not, by itself, transform the underlying conflict into an IAC, but it adds an international dimension. Israel provides a separate route: it has used force on Yemeni territory in response to Houthi attacks, and under the ICRC’s view, the unconsented use of force by one state against another state’s territory may itself create an IAC between them, even where the immediate target is a non-state armed group. Israeli strikes on Houthi-held territory could therefore support a parallel Israel-Yemen IAC. Do the Houthis, as a non-state armed group, have the legal authority to enforce a naval blockade? Iranian involvement provides another possible route to internationalisation. Arms, financing and political support alone are insufficient. Under the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia’s “overall control” test in Tadić, however, the threshold may be met where a state, beyond financing, training or equipping an organised armed group, also participates in planning its military activities; specific instructions for each operation are unnecessary. The ICJ’s stricter “effective control” test, relevant to attribution of particular conduct, requires proof that the state directed or controlled the specific operation in question. Accordingly, if the conflict is international, traditional blockade law is more readily applicable; if the Houthis remain solely a non-state party to an NIAC, their authority to impose blockade obligations on neutral shipping remains controversial. In either case, a declaration alone is insufficient: a blockade must satisfy the requirements of effectiveness, notification, impartiality and applicable humanitarian limitations. Regardless of classification, the Houthis are bound by applicable international humanitarian law. In an NIAC, Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions and applicable customary IHL apply; in an IAC, the Geneva Conventions apply in full, together with customary IHL. In either case, rules governing distinction, military goals, proportionality and precautions constrain the conduct of hostilities. The law of naval blockade is further governed by the law of armed conflict at sea and customary international law, as elaborated in the San Remo Manual. Under paragraphs 93-104, a blockade must be declared and notified to belligerents and neutral states; specify its commencement, duration, location and extent; allow neutral vessels an appropriate period to depart; be effective and impartially applied; and comply with humanitarian restrictions, including those concerning essential civilian supplies. Importantly, the Houthis have denied seeking to close Bab al-Mandeb to international navigation. Their spokesman stated that there was “no closure” of the strait and described the measure as a maritime blockade affecting only the Saudi side. The main legal question, therefore, is not whether the Houthis may close Bab al-Mandeb as a coastal authority, but whether they may lawfully impose and enforce a belligerent blockade against Saudi Arabia and shipping falling within its scope. Military necessity, however, does not independently make commercial shipping a lawful target. Article 52(2) of Additional Protocol I, reflecting the customary definition of a military objective, requires an object, by its nature, location, purpose or use, to make an effective contribution to military action and for its destruction, capture or neutralisation to offer a definite military advantage. Particular Saudi vessels, ports or assets directly supporting military operations may satisfy that test, but the general contribution of commercial trade to Saudi Arabia’s economy and war capacity does not, by itself, transform every merchant vessel into a military goal. Any attack remains subject to distinction, proportionality and precautions. This distinction is particularly important for neutral shipping. Neutral vessels do not lose protection merely because they trade with Saudi Arabia or indirectly contribute to its economy. Whether a vessel may lawfully be intercepted, cap­­tured or attacked must be determined under the specific rules governing blockade, neutral shipping and military objectives, rather than through a general invocation of military necessity. Finally, the simultaneous closure of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb would place roughly a quarter of global oil flows and a major share of LNG trade at risk. Some analysts view pressure on both chokepoints as part of a broader Iranian strategy, working through the Houthis to increase economic pressure on the US and its Gulf partners and create leverage over the wider war. Pakistan has condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia while continuing to stress diplomacy and regional de-escalation. It has so far avoided direct military involvement under the Makkah accord, maintaining a cautious approach that limits the risk of Pakistan being drawn into the widening regional conflict. The writer is a professor of law at Lums. Published in Dawn, September 27th, 2026

Inflation seen slowing to 10.75pc in September. KARACHI: Some stakeholders and analysts expect inflation in September to slow despite the high uncertainty caused by the ongoing Gulf war. The financial sector expects oil prices to remain between $90 and $100 per barrel during the remaining days of September and in October. However, the situation has once again changed after US President Donald Trump announced on Saturday that he had rejected Iran’s proposal for the Gulf war. Iran is now anticipating possible attacks from the US, raising concerns that oil prices could surge. Analysts expect oil prices to remain around $100 per barrel if the war resumes. However, much will depend on the availability of oil supplies in the international market. Pakistan imports 70pc of its oil and gas requirements, making inflation highly sensitive to oil prices. Stakeholders believe oil prices to hover around $100 per barrel Pakistan’s official headline inflation rose sharply to 11.1pc year-on-year in August 2026, up from 9.2pc in July 2026. According to a Topline Securities report, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for September is expected to rise 10.25-10.75pc year-on-year, down from 11.1pc in August. This projection is slightly lower than the August figure, but does not represent a significant decline. Petroleum prices have been rising daily in Pakistan and have now reached the highest level in the region. India increased petrol prices by 10pc, while Bangladesh reportedly jacked up by 16pc and Pakistan by over 50pc. “It is not easy to assess the exact inflation figure for September as oil prices have been changing both internationally and locally. We can only expect slightly lower inflation, with a fear that it may remain close to last month’s level,” said S.S. Iqbal, a money market expert. With inflation expected to remain at 10.25-10.75pc in September 2026, real interest rates are likely to stand at 75-125 basis points, lower than Pakistan’s historical average of 200-300 basis points, according to the Topline report. Electricity, housing, food and construction costs have also witnessed increases, suggesting that inflation could come in above analysts’ expectations, particularly if the Gulf war continues for an extended period. At the same time, Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia are preparing to respond to a possible new conflict involving the Houthis and the kingdom, adding to uncertainty over oil prices and supplies. Any disruption could have a direct impact on Pakistan’s economy and inflation. Pakistan’s foreign exchange reserves, currently exceeding $21.4 billion, may provide some cushion against higher oil import costs. However, they cannot prevent inflationary pressures from rising if the conflict continues and international energy prices remain elevated. Published in Dawn, September 27th, 2026

Hamas leader says Israel to campaign off Gaza's 'blood' in election. The leader of Hamas brushed aside the possibility of change from Israel’s upcoming election in an interview on Saturday, saying he expected Israelis to campaign off Gaza’s “blood”. “Whether this or that person comes to power, or this party or another — our people have suffered at the hands of all Israeli parties,” Khalil al-Hayya told the Qatari station Al-Araby. “We absolutely refuse to allow the blood, suffering, and cause of the Palestinian people to serve as fuel for Israeli elections. What matters to us is that our people achieve their goals, aspirations and legitimate rights.” Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is locked in a tight contest as he seeks to stay in power in the October 27 elections. The Israeli premier has vowed in the run-up to the vote not to withdraw troops from Gaza and rejected a US-led peace initiative in which Hamas said it would surrender weapons, a promise Israel views with scepticism. The vote is the first since Hamas led the attack against Israel on October 7, 2023. Israel’s retaliatory offensive has displaced virtually the entire population of Gaza, damaged or destroyed the vast majority of buildings and killed more than 73,900 people, according to the Gaza health ministry. Polls show Netanyahu’s most formidable challenger to be Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief who served in Netanyahu’s war cabinet but has accused him of failing strategically. ‘Ready to sit down’ with Abbas The Palestinian Authority in turn has scheduled a legislative election for November 28, which would be the first in two decades, although there are widespread doubts about whether it will go ahead. Hamas won the last election, held in 2006, defeating Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas’s Fatah. Abbas, 90, has since been ruling by decree, with the legislature not allowed to convene and Hamas seizing control of Gaza. Abbas is based in the West Bank, where the Palestinian Authority wields limited autonomy. “We are ready to sit down with President Abbas to lay the foundations for a national program and achieve genuine unity,” Hayya said. “If the Palestinian elections are postponed, that step must serve as an entry point for putting the Palestinian house in order.” Hamas has been working on an alliance with Mohammed Dahlan, a former Fatah figure born in Gaza who has been an interlocutor with the United States on its peace plan. “In the event of a postponement, the alliance will remain intact and open to all, aiming to forge a unified national front,” Hayya said. It remains uncertain if Hamas could even run in the election, as Abbas has required all candidates to accept the platform of the Palestine Liberation Organisation, which has recognised Israel’s right to exist since 1993 at the start of the Oslo peace accords. On the regional front, Hayaa said that Hamas had offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis, who have carried out escalating attacks against the kingdom since July. “I hope that this will be accepted,” he said of Hamas’s offer. “Hamas is loyal to these peoples, who are our base.”

China sends 2 giant pandas to US after Washington summit. China sent two giant pandas to the United States on Sunday, state media said, after a Washington summit that was heavy on symbolism and light on breakthroughs. The pandas’ transfer had already been agreed, but the departure was announced on Thursday during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington. The black and white mammals are immensely popular around the world, and China loans them out as part of a “panda diplomacy” programme to foster foreign ties. Ping Ping and Fu Shuang departed from Chengdu Shuangliu International Airport on a chartered flight at around 3:00 am on Sunday (12am PKT on Saturday), state news agency Xinhua reported. Steamed corn buns, bamboo shoots and carrots have been prepared to keep the pandas nourished during their 15-hour flight, Chinese state-run media outlet the Global Times reported. The Boeing 777 operated by FedEx was the top-tracked aircraft on aviation information platform FlightRadar24 as it neared Alaska, roughly halfway into its journey. The pandas are headed to a zoo in Atlanta, Georgia, where they will be spending the next 10 years. A farewell ceremony was held for the pair before their departure by the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding. Experienced keepers were dispatched by the US side to accompany the duo on their flight, the Global Times reported. In preparation for their arrival, Zoo Atlanta has renovated its panda facilities and assembled a team of animal caretakers. It has also ensured a stable and long-term supply of bamboo, grown locally in Atlanta, which has a climate that is very similar to Chengdu. Zoo Atlanta previously hosted pandas on loan from China for a quarter of a century starting in 1999, but it has not had any since 2024. Both the expected arrivals were born in 2020. Ping Ping, a male, is now six years old, while Fu Shuang, a female, will turn six next month. Pandas in captivity typically live for around 30 years. The furry creatures have been sent across the globe for decades as soft-power ambassadors of Beijing’s diplomatic goodwill. In 1972, China gifted a pair of pandas to Washington, following US President Richard Nixon’s historic visit. Beijing recalled two of its pandas from Japan early this year, following a diplomatic spat that began when Japan’s prime minister hinted that Tokyo could intervene militarily in the event of any attack on Taiwan.

'Protest everyone's right but minus Islamabad': Sanaullah says 'practice' of marches to capital should end. Prime Minister’s Adviser on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah contended on Saturday that everyone had a constitutional and legal right to protest, but Islamabad should be off-limits for demonstrations and urged people to “end the practice” of staging long marches and protests in the federal capital. PTI had been gearing up for a nationwide protest and march towards Islamabad to press for the release of its founder, Imran Khan, who is currently incarcerated in Rawalpindi’s Adiala jail. However, the party announced a day ago that the march has been postponed to Oct 4. Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) had also launched a march towards Islamabad against the petroleum levy, but it postponed the move at the request of PM Shehbaz Sharif, pending a meeting with him. “If anyone needs to protest, they can do so in Faisalabad, Hyderabad, Karachi, Peshawar, or Multan. This practice needs to end,” Sanaullah said on Geo News programme ‘Jirga’. He pointed out that the ban on protests in Islamabad did not apply only to the PTI. Gatherings in the capital without prior permission are also banned under the Peaceful Assembly and Public Order Act 2024 , which had been rushed through the National Assembly ahead of a PTI gathering that month. “Peaceful protest is everyone’s constitutional and legal right, but they need to minus Islamabad from that,” Sanaullah stated. “It is everyone’s right, but minus attacks on Islamabad. This must be ensured.” He highlighted that a message had been sent that no protests would be allowed within Islamabad, as foreign diplomats were present in the federal capital and demonstrations would send a “bad message”. The PML-N leader accused PTI of aiming to overthrow the government, alleging that their goal is to “erect ladders next to the walls of Adiala jail and break in to meet Imran Khan”, who has been incarcerated there since an Aug 5, 2023 conviction. “How is this peaceful?” Sanaullah asked. “Party leaders have been threatening to overthrow the government or free someone from jail and then go back,” he outlined. “Permission for a long march will not be granted if this is their intent.” The PM’s aide stressed that no streets in Islamabad, besides those in the Red Zone and the M-1 Motorway, were shut for traffic. He clarified that containers had only been placed “at the corners” of the city’s roads for “safety”. “There are containers on every corner of Islamabad, but as we speak right now, no roads have been closed with them,” he said, explaining that containers have been placed at those points so they can be deployed as and when needed. “The situation in Islamabad is not as it is being described in the media,” he asserted, noting that some were referring to the capital as a “container city”. The PM’s aide stressed that PTI also did not submit any application to the Islamabad administration seeking permission for a gathering, nor inform it of its expected time and duration. Sanaullah added that PTI should approach the Islamabad High Court (IHC) and provide their “required guarantees”, contending that they did not intend to do that. Asked if the authorities’ response to any march would be similar to the Nov 26, 2024 crackdown on PTI’s ’Final Call’ protest , Sanaullah said he did not want to “say any such thing” as there were fellow Pakistanis, friends and colleagues in the party. However, he warned that PTI “should not hold such a march at any cost that would attempt to push back law enforcement agencies and move towards D-Chowk”. “Under no circumstance will they be granted access,” Sanaullah warned, cautioning PTI supporters against using force, noting that such an action, in the wake of IHC’s recent ruling, would provide authorities with “legal backing” to respond. Hearing a plea against the planned march, the IHC on September 14 ruled that no political party or its leadership has the “lawful right to occupy public roads, highways, interchanges, toll plazas and buildings in Islamabad”. Meanwhile, in the Rawalpindi Division and the federal capital territory, security measures and preparations to deal with any emergency situation remain in place despite the postponement of the march. Punjab had already imposed a ban on gatherings across the province until Oct 5 and prohibited inciting people to “unlawful assembly”. A similar ban under Section 144 has been enforced in Islamabad for two months. The federal government has also approved the deployment of Rangers in Islamabad and several districts of Punjab from Sept 20 to Oct 5.

2 heavyweights emerge for NA-168 by-polls today. LAHORE: The Bahawalpur NA-168 by-election has turned into a contest between PML-N’s Malik Munir Iqbal Channar, the son of the deceased lawmaker, and independent candidate Wali Dad Cheema, the son of former federal minister Tariq Bashir Cheema. The polling on the constituency is scheduled for Sept 27 in which sympathy following the death of sitting PML-N MNA Malik Muhammad Iqbal Channar, demands for a separate province and the PTI’s decision to boycott the election have emerged as key features of the by-election. Whereas, the PPP had also withdrawn its candidate and announced support for Mr Channar, while other political and religious groups have also extended support to him. PPP leader Syed Ali Haider Gillani, while addressing the media, said that they were supporting PML-N under the coalition agreement. He said that PML-N had also not fielded its candidate on the seat won by the PPP in the 2024 election. On the other hand, PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan had said the party would not participate in any electoral process under the current circumstances. The decision has left the party without a candidate in the constituency despite its candidate Samiullah Chaudhry being the runner-up to the late Mr Channar in the 2024 general elections. Independent candidate Wali Dad Cheema has been openly appealing to PTI supporters and sympathisers to vote for him. Addressing a gathering, Mr Cheema said he had entered the contest because of the PTI boycott, otherwise the PML-N candidate would have won without an election. He said that he needed PTI supporters’ backing to win the contest. PTI has announced boycott of elections, while PPP has withdrawn its candidate in support of PML-N However, PTI leaders from different areas of Punjab have subsequently posted videos on social media rejecting claims that the party or its supporters were backing the Cheema group. They have urged their supporters to abstain from voting. Several voters interviewed by Dawn said the death of Mr Channar has generated sympathy for his family and could translate into support for his son. A voter, Mustafa Khan, said the Channar clan appeared united behind the PML-N candidate following the death of his father. “Although the candidate was not very popular among the masses and his father had not given him a provincial assembly ticket, his position is still good,” he said. Mr Khan said Mr Tariq Bashir Cheema had not contested an election for around 18 years in this constituency and could therefore find it difficult to mobilise substantial support. He also referred to controversies surrounding Wali Dad Cheema. Another voter, Khadim Hussain, said the demand for a Seraiki province could benefit the Channar candidate because the Cheema camp was campaigning for the restoration of the Bahawalpur province. He said he would personally vote for a candidate who supported the demand for a Seraiki province. Social activist Salman Bhadera also described Mr Channar’s position as favourable, saying PML-N local leaders and a group of around 15 MPAs were holding gatherings to mobilise support for the candidate. He said people in Bahawalpur generally supported candidates who visited them and sought votes respectfully. He alleged that Mr Cheema and his supporters had adopted a confrontational approach and were issuing threats and challenging local political norms, which, he argued, could work against them. When asked about the possible disposition of PTI supporters, he said they were not fully prepared to support any particular candidate. According to Mr Bhadera, PML-N was seeking to mobilise its workers while Mr Cheema was attempting to consolidate support through his personal contacts and political groups. He said that only PTI was popular and the candidate who managed to get their support could win easily. On the other hand, Wali Dad Cheema and his father have repeatedly campaigned for restoring the Bahawalpur province and have maintained that Bahawalpur should be made a province regardless of whether the government created other provinces. The issue has gained significance because the PPP, while supporting the PML-N candidate, has also publicly expressed support for the creation of new provinces, including a Seraiki province. For voters, however, the campaign remains centred on a combination of local representation, political alliances, provincial status and constituency-level concerns. Leonardo MUNOZ / AFP Special Briefing 15 / Multilateral Diplomacy 14 September 2026 20+ minutes Ten Challenges for the UN in 2026-2027 As the 2026 General Assembly begins, the UN remains hobbled by cost cutting and big-power wrangling. The new Secretary-General to be chosen soon cannot cure all that ails the organisation, but much can be done to put its still considerable capacity to work. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print "> Download PDF Full Report (en) Related Tags Global What’s new? Leaders gathering at the UN General Assembly will find an organisation in need of revival. UN diplomacy aimed at halting wars and easing civilian suffering remains paralysed, while funding cuts have weakened UN capacity. States have one eye to the future as they prepare to appoint a new Secretary-General. Why does it matter? The UN remains the only universal forum for global cooperation on war and peace, even as the international order it anchors is under mounting strain. Many member states hope the next Secretary-General can help the organisation dispel its malaise and forge a new direction. What should be done? A new Secretary-General cannot resolve the world’s crises overnight, but this person should work with member states to address immediate challenges. High on the list should be bolstering the UN’s peacemaking and conflict management capabilities, mobilising political and financial support, and making a renewed case for international cooperation. I. Overview When world leaders last met at the UN General Assembly in September 2025, the organisation was in disarray, reeling from U.S. aid freezes and major-power disputes. A year on, the organisation remains trapped in an open-ended crisis, even after an additional round of cost cutting and other reforms. Under the Trump administration, the U.S. has morphed from a flawed champion of the international legal order into an overt scofflaw. While the U.S. has not repudiated the multilateral system anchored by the UN, it has done great damage to the organisation, insisting on shrinking multilateral peace operations, slow-rolling funding and tried to impose its ideological agenda. The Security Council continues to be a forum for hashing out big-power differences – with the U.S., Russia and China coming to agreement on second-tier files. But as regards the most salient peace and security challenges today – the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, as well as Ukraine and Sudan – the UN is notable mainly for being stuck. The next Secretary-General cannot cure all that ails the UN, but creative diplomacy could be useful in putting its still considerable capacity to work. If the overall mood at the UN is one of drifting toward perdition, it is partly because everyone is waiting for change at the top of the system. Secretary-General António Guterres will complete his term at the end of December. A small batch of candidates – eight, at the time of writing – have been publicly and privately lobbying throughout the year to replace him. Most have been cautious in their campaigning, to avoid offending the major powers that dominate the selection process. UN insiders are watching with mixed feelings. Some hope that the next Secretary-General can bring new energy to the organisation and, assuming Washington is amenable, restore a measure of political relevance and financial stability. Others worry that the U.S., China and Russia will connive to choose a weak candidate firmly under their control and that the Trump administration will force the next UN chief to make even more radical cuts throughout the institution. The selection process has at least focused minds on what the UN, multilateral cooperation and international law exist to achieve. Many member states have emphasised that they would like to see the incoming Secretary-General do more to promote conflict prevention and resolution, which Guterres has sometimes given short shrift while pursuing other goals, such as international cooperation on artificial intelligence. Guterres no doubt felt that he had little to gain by focusing on geopolitical crises given the lack of consensus among the big powers. But there is now a widespread sense that the UN cannot pretend to be a useful platform for discussions of far-reaching issues like AI if governments do not believe that it can deliver on its core, UN Charter-defined purpose of maintaining peace and security. The crises of the last twelve months have also offered reminders of the extent to which the UN still offers a necessary if imperfect scaffolding for international cooperation. The Trump administration has grudgingly turned to the Security Council to endorse its conflict management efforts in Haiti and Gaza. Faced with the fallout of the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran, such as closure of the Strait of Hormuz, governments around the world have stressed the importance of international legal principles including the prohibition of aggressive war, rules protecting civilians and civilian objects in conflict, and freedom of navigation. Though the UN has had a vanishingly small voice in diplomacy aimed at ending the Middle East war, both U.S. and Iranian officials have acknowledged that the Security Council should play some role – if only a ministerial one – in any peace deal. The UN ... remains best positioned to deliver humanitarian aid, mount peace operations and manage protracted crises that few other actors ... can handle. These are small consolations, but at a moment in which the U.S. and Russia are learning the limits of hard power in the Middle East and Ukraine, there is still space to reiterate the case for diplomacy, cooperation and respect for law. The next UN Secretary-General can make it. While it is foolish to expect a single administrator, however senior, to save the world, many small and midsize UN member states, as well as many major-power officials, are ready to heed a call to reinforce the lapsing international legal order. The UN also remains best positioned to deliver humanitarian aid, mount peace operations and manage protracted crises that few other actors – including the flailing U.S.-backed Board of Peace – can handle. It is possible that new leadership at the UN can give the organisation as a whole, and its peace and security pillar in particular, a new strategic direction. But amid deadly violence, regional rifts and institutional headaches, it is a near certainty that UN crisis management will continue to involve a great deal of firefighting and muddling through. This briefing, based on Crisis Group’s research at the UN and in the countries concerned, offers a guide to some of the most urgent issues. II. The Year in Review: Trends in UN Diplomacy The UN spent much of the past year adapting to a more assertive and transactional U.S. administration. Alongside long-running crises in Ukraine, Gaza and Sudan, the latest U.S.-Israeli war with Iran placed additional strain on Council diplomacy and the UN-backed international order. 1 Crisis Group Special Briefing N°14, Causes of Peace in an Era of Hard Power , 8 July 2026. Meanwhile, the UN’s multi-year liquidity crisis worsened, compounded by the U.S. aid cuts, disrupting operations at headquarters in New York and in the field. Steep reductions in voluntary contributions to UN humanitarian agencies forced the organisation to make difficult choices with its assistance, leaving many civilians affected by armed conflict with little support. Debates over the UN’s future simmered as member states began their search for the next Secretary-General. A year after Donald Trump’s return to the White House, the organisation was no longer in shock but adjusting to a new normal. A. Crisis Management and UN Diplomacy 1. The Security Council A year ago, Crisis Group observed that U.S. diplomacy at the Security Council under the newly installed Trump administration had lacked a clear direction. 2 Crisis Group Special Briefing N°13, Ten Challenges for the UN in 2025-2026 , 9 September 2025. The arrival of U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz in New York on the eve of the 2025 UN General Assembly marked the beginning of a more purposeful, and often determined, U.S. approach in the Council. Together with Panama, the U.S. secured Council authorisation for a new Gang Suppression Force for Haiti shortly after Waltz’s arrival, along with a UN logistics office to defray some of the Force’s costs (see Section III.4). 3 “ Haiti: Vote on a Draft Resolution Authorizing a ‘Gang Suppression Force’ and a UN Support Office* ”, Security Council Report, 30 September 2025; Daniel Forti, “ New Force to Battle Haiti’s Gangs Gets Security Council Blessing ”, Crisis Group Analyst’s Notebook, 1 October 2025; Crisis Group Latin America & Caribbean Report N°110, Undoing Haiti’s Deadly Gang Alliance , 15 December 2025. Less than two months later, the Trump administration – backed by its regional partners and Palestine – persuaded the Council to endorse its ceasefire plan for Gaza and establish the vaguely defined Board of Peace. 4 “Resolution 2803”, UNSC S/RES/2803, 17 November 2025; Daniel Forti, Richard Gowan and Max Rodenbeck, “ What to Look for as the Gaza Peace Plan Comes to the UN Security Council ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 14 November 2025. In both cases, the Council agreed to arrangements that concentrated decision-making authority in Washington and minimised the UN’s political and operational roles. With UN diplomacy on the war in Gaza lowered to a simmer (see Section III.3), the U.S.-Iran conflict became the Council’s defining crisis of the past year. Major-power tensions over Iran were already high at the UN prior to the outbreak of hostilities at the end of February. After the breakdown of nuclear diplomacy between the U.S. and Iran in 2025 and the twelve-day campaign launched by Israel (and joined by the U.S.) against Iran in June, France, Germany and the UK – three of the participants in the 2015 nuclear deal, or Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action – decided to reimpose “snapback” sanctions on Tehran that were otherwise set to expire that October. 5 Naysan Rafati and Daniel Forti, “ Iran Sanctions Snapback at the UN ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 25 August 2026. Beijing and Moscow rejected the legality of the reimposed UN sanctions, and in protest, they have obstructed business in all of the Council’s sanctions committees and thematic working groups since 2026 began. 6 China and Russia have blocked the appointment of the chairs and vice chairs of all subsidiary bodies, which require Council unanimity according to the body’s informal working methods. The chairs and vice chairs are responsible for leading each body’s meetings, briefing the Council on behalf of each body and managing its workflow. For more, see “ In Hindsight: A Second Year of Delays in the Allocation of Subsidiary Body Chairs ”, Security Council Report, 1 July 2026; Letter from the Security Council’s ten elected members , UNSC S/2026/636, 30 July 2026. Tensions in the Council gradually escalated after the U.S. and Israel once again attacked Iran on 28 February. Tensions in the Council gradually escalated after the U.S. and Israel once again attacked Iran on 28 February. China and Russia sharply criticised the two states during the Council’s first emergency meeting on the war. But even so they allowed passage of a Bahrain-led resolution condemning Iran’s retaliatory fire at its Gulf Arab neighbours days later, abstaining instead of vetoing it. Their posture suggested that preserving relations with the Gulf states was a higher priority than blocking a one-sided resolution that had no teeth. 7 Beijing and Moscow abstained from the vote. Russia also submitted a separate counter-resolution discussing the war’s root causes that got too few votes to be adopted. See “ Resolution 2817 ”, UNSC S/RES/2817, 11 March 2026. Their stances gradually hardened, however, as Washington pressed the Security Council to consider more coercive measures against Tehran. In early April, the Gulf states and the U.S. tabled a resolution for the Council to endorse a vaguely defined multinational naval coalition that would be tasked with reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Moscow and Beijing vetoed the text despite intense lobbying by Gulf capitals, arguing that the resolution would have given the U.S. open-ended authorisation to escalate its campaign. 8 The vote took place hours after U.S. President Donald Trump shared a social media message threatening to annihilate Iran. During its explanation of vote, Russia invoked the Security Council’s 2011 open-ended authorisation of NATO-led military action in Libya as a comparison to the proposed Gulf-U.S. initiative. Crisis Group interviews, UN diplomats, April-May 2026. See also remarks by the Russian Federation, “ Provisional Verbatim of the 10130th meeting of the United Nations Security Council”, UNSC S/PV.10130, 7 April 2026. Weeks later, the U.S. and Gulf states drafted another resolution to demand that Iran open and demine the strait, while threatening sanctions for non-compliance. Despite finding over 138 co-sponsors, the U.S. and Bahrain did not submit the text for a vote, as they could not secure the support of Russia and China. Council diplomacy on the file has since stalled. Complex and sometimes volatile relations among the U.S., China, and Russia continue to shape the boundaries of Council diplomacy beyond the Gulf. After the reversal of U.S. Ukraine policy in early 2025, when the Trump administration stopped sending arms to Kyiv to resist Russia’s all-out invasion, Moscow may have expected Washington to press the Ukrainian government to make concessions in negotiations to end the fighting. Instead, U.S. statements in the Security Council have criticised Russia’s full-scale invasion and called on the Kremlin to agree to an immediate ceasefire. 9 Remarks by the United States, “ Provisional Verbatim of the 10166th Meeting of the United Nations Security Council ”, UNSC S/PV.10166, 8 June 2026. More often than not, U.S. and Russian diplomats have sparred over UN responses to crises in the Middle East and Africa. By contrast, Washington and Beijing have shown willingness to strike occasional deals in the Security Council. Though they frequently clash, recent Council action has depended on a degree of cooperation between these geopolitical rivals. In September 2025, the U.S. agreed to pay nearly $680 million to the UN peacekeeping budget and drop its objections to China becoming penholder on the Council’s Afghanistan file in exchange for Beijing’s support for the Gang Suppression Force in Haiti. 10 Daniel Forti and Richard Gowan, “ Reading the Signals of China’s U.N. Security Council Role in the Afghanistan Mission Renewal ”, Just Security , 31 July 2026. More recently, China and the U.S. collaborated to streamline the mandate of the UN political office in Afghanistan and approved each other’s candidates for leadership posts in UN missions in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and South Sudan. Other Council members have found it harder to haggle with – much less criticise – the Trump administration’s adventurism. Unusually, several elected members have found themselves directly implicated in issues before the Council in 2026 to date. The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Somalia sought to preserve ties with the U.S. while influencing Council discussions on conflicts in their own countries. 16 Kinshasa has used its elected term on the Security Council to raise the profile of the conflict in the eastern DRC, while Mogadishu has sought to end the Council’s engagement with the war in Somalia. Denmark and Panama, meanwhile, have had to contend with Trump’s threats to annex Greenland and seize the Panama Canal, even as they maintained working relations with U.S. diplomats in New York. Bahrain assumed a more prominent role following Iran’s attacks on Gulf states, in close coordination with Washington. Colombia (under President Gustavo Petro, now out of office) and Pakistan, by contrast, have taken more critical positions on U.S. military actions. Whereas previous cohorts of elected members had found common ground in pressing Washington for a ceasefire in Gaza, the present elected ten are less unified in how to conduct diplomacy with Washington. As for UN peace operations, where Washington sees clear strategic interests at stake, such as in the DRC and South Sudan, it has been willing to preserve UN missions and, at times, moderate its normally reflexive opposition to human rights, gender and climate-related activities – including where it has been stubborn in other mandate negotiations in the Security Council and General Assembly. More often, the U.S. has sought to scale back UN operations, claiming concerns about their effectiveness and costs. The Secretary-General Secretary-General Guterres has spent much of his final year in office trying to forestall the UN’s urgent financial crisis (discussed below), complete reforms under the UN80 initiative that he launched in 2025 and defend the UN Charter in response to violations by two permanent members, Russia and the U.S. 21 The UN80 initiative, launched by Guterres in March 2025, is premised on three separate reform processes. The first is premised on budget cuts and cost savings at the UN Secretariat; the second features a review of all inter-governmental mandates; and the third is anchored in proposals for larger institutional reforms (including proposals to merge different UN agencies and offices). “ UN80 Initiative ”, UN, August 2026. Neither Moscow nor Washington is eager to engage with him personally, curtailing his opportunities to pursue new diplomatic efforts. But the Secretary-General’s cautious outlook toward UN-led conflict management has left many diplomats and officials searching for a successor who will put the organisation’s work on peace and security front and centre. The Secretary-General’s limited influence over the past year has not always been due to a lack of initiative. Shortly after the resumption of hostilities between the U.S. and Iran, Guterres appealed for creating a humanitarian corridor to permit the passage of fuel and fertiliser through the Strait of Hormuz, established a UN mechanism modelled on the Black Sea Grain Initiative to facilitate these efforts and appointed a personal envoy to boost the UN’s diplomatic response. 22 “ Note to Correspondents: on the Strait of Hormuz ”, UN, 27 March 2026. His focus on the war’s global consequences won plaudits but failed to have meaningful impact, as neither the Gulf states nor the U.S. showed serious interest in reopening the strait, except in full and without condition. The initiative has faded from memory even as the war has reignited and traffic through the waterway remains constrained. 23 Guterres shared a brief update about the UN mechanism at a 24 August press conference. See “ Secretary-General’s Press Encounter – On the United Nations’ Efforts to Uphold Navigational Rights and Freedoms ”, Office of the UN Secretary-General, 24 August 2026. Elsewhere, Guterres has deployed his dwindling political capital selectively. At the end of July, he travelled to Cyprus to revive his long-running mediation between Greek and Turkish Cypriots. He also made personal appeals to Sudan’s belligerents in support of a proposed humanitarian ceasefire in Darfur. The Secretary-General continued to press for Security Council reform, including at a high-level summit convened by France and Kenya in May, and in August he released a long-awaited review of UN peace operations mandated by the 2024 Pact for the Future (see Section III.9). 24 “ Review on the future of all forms of United Nations Peace Operations ”, UNGA A/80/798 – UNSC S/2026/600, 22 July 2026. Yet meaningful progress on these and other such priorities has eluded him. B. UN Reform The UN’s financial outlook has deteriorated sharply over the past year, largely due to Washington’s failure to pay its fair share. Since President Trump returned to office, the U.S. has ponied up only a portion of the nearly $4 billion in dues it owes the organisation. 25 In late August, the U.S. agreed to make a payment of $725 million to the UN regular budget, an amount reportedly calculated by Washington to avoid losing its vote in the General Assembly under Article 19 of the UN Charter. The U.S. is not the only member state withholding its obligatory dues, even if it is the largest and has accumulated the most arrears. China has regularly delayed its annual payments to the UN regular budget – in 2026 paying only at the beginning of September – though it traditionally does not accumulate arrears. See Catherine Pollard, “ Financial situation of the United Nations ”, statement to the Fifth Committee of the General Assembly at its 80th Session, 7 May 2026; “ Chandramouli Ramanathan (UN Controller) & others on the UN Budget ”, Office of the UN Spokesperson, 1 July 2026; Humeyra Pamuk and Emma Farge, “ US plans $725 million payment towards its large UN debt ”, Reuters, 21 August 2026. U.S. officials have openly stated their intention to place the UN on a starvation diet and withdrawn from several UN bodies. 26 “ Withdrawing the United States from International Organizations, Conventions and Treaties that Are Contrary to the Interests of the United States ”, White House, 7 January 2026; Emma Farge, Olivia Le Poidevin, Simon Lewis and David Brunnstrom, “ Diplomatic efforts seek to avert Trump split with UN refugee agency, sources say ”, Reuters, 21 July 2026. Yet, to the relief of many diplomats and UN officials, Washington no longer appears intent on a wholesale retreat from the organisation. Since the end of 2025, it has provided nearly $5 billion in voluntary funding to Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), UNICEF and the World Food Programme, agencies that have embraced the administration’s reform agenda and retained bipartisan support in Congress. While these contributions have been critical in sustaining key UN operations, they remain well below Washington’s historical level of support and are heavily earmarked to align with U.S. priorities. 27 “ OCHA-Managed Humanitarian Funds Receive Landmark US$2 Billion Contribution from United States ”, UN OCHA, 29 December 2025; “ United States Pledges Additional $1.8 Billion in Life-Saving Humanitarian Funding to OCHA’s Humanitarian Reset & Shares Powerful Results from the Trump Administration’s UN Humanitarian Reform Agreement ”, U.S. Department of State, 14 May 2026; “ United States Announces More Than $1 Billion in Assistance to UNICEF and World Food Program to Address Global Humanitarian Needs ”, U.S. Department of State, 16 June 2026. C. The Search for a New Secretary-General The process of choosing Guterres’ successor, which began in November 2025, is approaching a crescendo. Members of the Security Council held their first straw poll at the end of July, and they will continue to take these informal soundings until one candidate receives at least nine votes from the fifteen-member body with no objection from any of the five permanent members. Eight candidates are in the running. They are: Ivonne A-Baki (former Ecuadorian ambassador to France and the U.S.), Michelle Bachelet (former president of Chile and head of UN Women), María Fernanda Espinosa Garcés (former foreign minister of Ecuador and president of the 73rd General Assembly), Rafael Grossi (director-general of the International Atomic Energy Agency), Rebeca Grynspan (former second vice president of Costa Rica and head of the UN Conference on Trade and Development), Olara Otunnu (former Ugandan foreign minister and former UN representative for children and armed conflict), Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett (Guyana’s permanent representative to the UN) and Macky Sall (former president of Senegal). 39 María Fernanda Espinosa Garcés currently serves on Crisis Group’s Board of Trustees. Rumours abound of others weighing entering the race, and many diplomats lament that their preferences may well be in vain since those of the five permanent members will be decisive in the race’s outcome. 40 Colum Lynch, “ Are we headed for big power stitch up in race for UN leader? ”, Devex, 26 June 2026. Ten Challenges for the UN Even as the UN is mired in interlocking difficulties, the organisation can still contribute to conflict resolution and crisis management in many domains. The following list features countries and issue areas where the UN confronts either major challenges or opportunities in the year ahead. It is intended to demonstrate the myriad factors affecting how the UN and its member states respond to conflicts and emergencies around the world. The list is not exhaustive, however, and it excludes cases that Crisis Group has highlighted elsewhere or in years past, such as Afghanistan, the DRC, South Sudan, Ukraine and others. 1. Continuing UN engagement in southern Lebanon In August 2025, the U.S. and Israel strong-armed the Security Council into shutting down the UN peacekeeping mission in southern Lebanon (UNIFIL) – first established in 1978 and significantly upgraded by Resolution 1701 twenty years ago – by the end of 2026 (though the phased withdrawal of troops will extend considerably past 31 December). 50 “ Resolution 2790 ”, UNSC S/RES/2790, 28 August 2025. While questions about southern Lebanon have long vexed the Council, the latest conflagration between Israel and Hizbollah raises the stakes even higher. 51 Heiko Wimmen and David Wood, “ Entrenching a Meaningful Israel-Lebanon Ceasefire ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 19 June 2026. The danger is now that the UN will terminate its 48-year blue helmet operation without clarity on what kind of international presence, if any, might follow. Much will now depend on the trajectory of U.S.-backed negotiations between Israel and Lebanon, which to date have failed to produce a viable security arrangement. The two states signed a “framework agreement” on 26 June, under which the Lebanese army is to assert control of “pilot zones” in southern Lebanon, ensuring that Hizbollah no longer has a military footprint in these areas. 52 “ Trilateral Framework Between the United States of America, the State of Israel and the Republic of Lebanon ”, U.S. Department of State, 26 June 2026. Yet the scheme, which is meant to “serve as the mechanism for phased and verified (Israeli) redeployments”, has already run into trouble. 53 Ibid. Lebanon complains that Israel has kept attacking Lebanese territory, including with lethal airstrikes and the systematic destruction of villages, and authorised “pilot zones” only in areas that it never occupied. Israeli officials, for their part, make Hizbollah’s full disarmament a condition for the Israeli army’s withdrawal. 54 Maayan Lubell and Maya Gebeily, “ After US criticism, Israel ties Lebanon withdrawal to Hezbollah disarmament ”, Reuters, 13 August 2026. Beirut officially outlawed Hizbollah’s military activities in March, but, in practice, it cannot risk trying to compel the group to disarm. 55 Lebanese political and military leaders have resisted calls to deploy the Lebanese army to confront Hizbollah by force. They fear that such a move could trigger disastrous domestic consequences, such as the military fracturing along sectarian lines. Crisis Group Middle East Briefing N°94, Containing Domestic Tensions in War-hit Lebanon , 27 February 2025. See also Michael Young, “ Pushing Beirut into an armed conflict with Hezbollah is insane ”, Diwan (blog), Carnegie Middle East Center, 14 May 2026. Even if the terms of the deal were to be spelled out more precisely, the belligerents would almost certainly refuse to sign up to the underlying bargain. Hizbollah rejects the direct Israel-Lebanon negotiations outright, insisting that Lebanon entrust Iran, the group’s patron, with securing a full Israeli withdrawal as part of Tehran’s negotiations with Washington. 56 “ Hezbollah insists on linking Lebanon to Iran-U.S. negotiations ”, Asharq al-Awsat , 13 July 2026. Though Israel has participated in the trilateral talks with Lebanon and the U.S., it refuses to accept another arrangement like Resolution 1701, under which its troops withdrew from Lebanon after the 2006 war while Hizbollah remained under arms. Debates about a future international presence will also be shaped by U.S. and Israeli scepticism. Israel has long questioned the value of UNIFIL in helping Lebanon constrain Hizbollah, and it has shown little appetite for a replacement that might obstruct its own military operations. The U.S. does not oppose an international mission per se, but it is wary of replicating a UNIFIL model that it deems ineffective. 57 Crisis Group interviews, diplomats and UN officials, Beirut, July 2026. The U.S. and its Israeli partners have long argued that UNIFIL has failed to deter Hizbollah military operations south of the Litani River (even if it has no mandate to confront the militant group by force) and is too expensive. For background, see David Wood, “ Helping UNIFIL Restore Stability in Southern Lebanon ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 14 August 2025. Washington has sidelined the monitoring mechanism attached to the November 2024 ceasefire, in which UNIFIL and France (the Council’s penholder on Lebanon) were represented. Instead, an annex of the June framework agreement provides for a U.S.-headed “military coordination group”, through which Israel and Lebanon will manage tasks that UNIFIL or a successor force might have helped tackle, including “deconfliction, verification and overall implementation”. 58 The parties did not officially release this annex to the framework agreement, but they have not challenged the authenticity of a text leaked to the media in late June. “ The Lebanon-Israel ‘security’ annex agreement revealed ”, L’Orient Today , 29 June 2026. Other Council members and Lebanon strongly favour retaining an international presence, having reluctantly agreed to UNIFIL’s termination at the end of 2026 to avoid a U.S. veto that would have abruptly ended the mission in August 2025. 59 “ UN Interim Force in Lebanon: Vote on Final Mandate Renewal and Drawdown* ”, Security Council Report, 28 August 2025; Jamie Prentis, “ Lebanese MPs urge UN to extend peacekeeping mission ”, The National , 24 July 2026. The framework agreement does not mention the UN or Security Council resolution 1701. The annex, however, proposes a future role for a “mutually agreed-upon third-party entity” to verify that non-state armed groups have been cleared from each “pilot zone”. 60 “ The Lebanon-Israel ‘security’ annex agreement revealed ”, op. cit. To date, Israeli, Lebanese and U.S. negotiators have struggled to flesh out what such verification would entail, making it difficult for interested nations to commit troops to a mission that might prove dangerous.
